title: Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM
gist: In this podcast a Red Hat engineer explains why distributed LLM inference needs cache-aware routing (llm-d on top of vLLM) rather than standard Kubernetes load balancing, and argues enterprises can own their AI on affordable hardware using right-sized models. He also covers Wasm as a sandboxing runtime and TornadoVM for running Java on GPUs.

themes.theme: Why LLM serving needs cache-aware routing

insights.claim: vLLM maximizes throughput on a single machine through PagedAttention and continuous batching, but scaling beyond one box requires routing requests across multiple vLLM instances.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Single-node engines hit a ceiling, creating a market for cluster-level inference orchestration.

insights.claim: Standard Kubernetes round-robin routing degrades LLM performance because inference is effectively stateful: chat and agentic sessions benefit from sticking to the same instance to reuse KV and prefix caches, yet sticking forever overloads it.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Cache locality versus load balance is the core scheduling tradeoff in inference infrastructure.
insights.quote: So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches
insights.locator: If you do it the traditional way

insights.claim: llm-d is a family of projects (scheduler, batch inference, routing) designed to keep expensive GPUs near full utilization, and the speaker says it reached 1.0, is production-ready, and is already used by companies, with Red Hat partnering with NVIDIA.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Vendor-aligned claim of maturity; signals open-source inference orchestration standardizing around Kubernetes.

insights.claim: LLMs are fundamentally stateless because every request resends the whole conversation, and cached-token pricing differs from uncached because a cache hit lets the model compute only the continuation rather than the entire prompt.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Explains the economics behind cached-token pricing and why cache-aware routing lowers costs.
insights.locator: The reason is, if you don't do a cached response

insights.claim: llm-d adds quality-of-service and prioritization of HTTP requests that vLLM lacked, so it can help even with a single instance or on bare metal outside Kubernetes.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Broadens addressable use beyond large clusters.
insights.locator: vLLM does not do automatic flow control

insights.claim: llm-d's batch inference runs background jobs when the cluster is underused, so scarce GPUs reach close to 100% utilization, which the speaker frames as key because the hardware is expensive whether owned or rented.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Utilization of idle GPU time is a direct cost lever for on-prem AI.
insights.locator: Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load.

insights.claim: llm-d relies on vLLM metrics for routing, which gives operators observability into tokens produced, failures, throughput and cluster saturation, with knobs to add machines or throttle requests.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Inference-level observability is becoming part of the infrastructure stack.
insights.locator: Yes, so I mean, it depends. It's a very wide question.

insights.claim: Accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google and startups have different programming languages, so a GPU kernel cannot be written once for every accelerator, which is why a framework layer like vLLM is needed.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Software abstraction layers become strategic as hardware diversifies away from NVIDIA.
insights.quote: you can't write the kernel for a GPU computation once and target every single accelerator there is because everything is different
insights.locator: Ah. Everything. Well, one thing that is interesting

insights.claim: Moving trillion-parameter model data across machines requires expensive high-speed interconnect such as RDMA in addition to expensive GPUs.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Networking is a significant cost component of distributed inference.
insights.locator: The other thing that is also possibly challenging

insights.claim: The speaker hopes more competition in accelerators, including startup chips, will eventually lower prices, though it currently complicates sourcing and software support.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Hardware competition could ease the GPU cost burden if software portability improves.
insights.locator: Hopefully it might make things more affordable

insights.claim: Expensive hardware is no longer required for decent inference quality: the speaker runs a 27B-parameter open model on a 48 GB Mac and says a modestly larger server could serve many requests efficiently.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Capable open models on commodity hardware weaken the case for always paying for frontier APIs.
insights.locator: I have a relatively beefy Mac myself

insights.claim: The speaker cautions against social-media hype that older models are no longer useful, noting a recent Qwen 27B model has been compared to Opus 4.6, which was impressive only a year ago.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Mid-tier and older models remain economically viable, pressuring frontier pricing.
insights.quote: let's not get too carried away by all the announcements we read on social media
insights.locator: So, if you get a server that is only slightly bigger

insights.claim: Running inference on owned hardware lets companies avoid sharing data with a third party they may not trust, and the speaker says this is especially true for companies rather than consumers.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Data-privacy motives support an on-premises AI infrastructure market.
insights.quote: You can own your own AI, you can own your own token inference
insights.locator: The old model are still useful

insights.claim: llm-d Semantic Classifier, incubating alongside the vLLM Semantic Router, routes each prompt to the right-sized model based on cost or topic, so large models are used only when needed and specialized fine-tuned small models handle the rest.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Model routing is a cost-optimization layer that shifts spend from frontier to smaller models.

insights.claim: The host argues that production deployments require refinement and efficiency rather than frontier models for everything, and that many teams are still measuring things that do not matter.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Production AI spend should shift toward efficiency and narrow models.
insights.locator: And at the point where you're getting into the production space

insights.claim: WebAssembly on the backend has become more relevant than during the hype phase because of sandboxing, cross-language compilation of one codebase, and live migration of workloads between browser and end-user devices, which suits agentic workloads.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Sandboxing demand from agents revives interest in Wasm runtimes.
insights.locator: State of WebAssembly on the Backend

insights.claim: Small language models are feasible in WebAssembly because it runs on CPUs first, but larger LLMs suit highly parallel GPUs, though experiments exist to translate WebAssembly into GPU kernels.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: In-browser inference is limited to small models.
insights.locator: WebAssembly is meant to run on the CPU first.

insights.claim: TornadoVM compiles Java code on the fly into GPU kernels such as PTX for NVIDIA and SPIR-V, enabling a GPU Llama 3 implementation written entirely in Java, though code must follow TornadoVM's style and cannot run Spring on the GPU.
insights.speaker: Edoardo Vacchi
insights.so_what: Java-native GPU compute widens the pool of developers able to build inference workloads.
insights.locator: TornadoVM: Translating Java Code to GPU Kernels
